title: The Quit-Proof Blueprint
summary: A simple plan to get your key person's knowledge out of their head and into a checklist, then automate the repeat parts. Built for small shops with no spare time.

sections.heading: 1. Find what lives in one head
points: List every task only one person does. Start with invoices, follow-ups, reporting and supplier orders.
Ask: if this person vanished today, what would break first?
Write down every login and tool they use. Note who actually owns each account.
Flag the odd rules, like 'this client always pays late' or 'never email this supplier on Fridays'.
Rank the list by pain. Fix the top three first, not all twenty.

sections.heading: 2. Capture it in one week
points: Ask them to record their screen while doing each task once, talking out loud. Most laptops and phones have a built-in screen recorder, or use a free tool like Loom.
Keep each recording to one task. Short beats thorough.
Turn each recording into a checklist: numbered steps, plain words, one action per line.
Have someone else follow the checklist cold. Wherever they get stuck, the checklist is missing a step.
Store everything in one shared folder that more than one person can open.

sections.heading: 3. Decide what to automate
points: Good candidates: repeatable, rule-based, same steps every time. Examples: creating an invoice from a form, sending a payment reminder, copying order details into a sheet.
Keep human: pricing exceptions, upset clients, anything needing judgment or tact.
Test each step with one question: could I explain this to a stranger using only if/then rules? If yes, automate it.
Start with one task. A small win you trust beats a big build you don't.

sections.heading: 4. Build your first Make.com scenario
points: Pick a trigger: a new form response, a new row in Google Sheets, or a new email.
Add the action: create the document, send the message, or update the row.
Run it with test data before touching anything real.
Turn on error notifications so a failure pings you instead of silently breaking.
Write one line in the checklist: 'This step is now done by the scenario. If it fails, do it by hand like this.'

sections.heading: 5. What to watch for
points: Shared access: put logins in a password manager such as Bitwarden or 1Password, not in one person's head or a sticky note.
Do this while your employee is happy and still here, not in the last week of a notice period.
Position it as backup for the whole team, not a plan to replace anyone.
Review the checklists every few months. Processes drift.
Notice periods and contracts vary, so check yours so you know how much time you would actually have.

title: The Cashless Shop Checklist
summary: A practical checklist to make paying at your shop faster, offer split payments safely, and log every sale without typing. Based on one mall visit, so treat it as ideas to test.

sections.heading: What I saw, and what I can't claim
points: Zara was packed. LC Waikiki, H&M and Max were nearly empty. That is one visit, not data.
Payments were cashless: QR codes, phones and a palm scan.
The app name I kept hearing was Kaspi. Look up how it describes itself.
My guess is that fast, easy paying makes big prices feel smaller. It is a guess, not a finding.
Skip country rankings. 'Developed' means different things on different lists.

sections.heading: Step 1: Make paying take two seconds
points: Time your own checkout from 'ready to pay' to 'receipt'. Write the number down.
Ask five regular customers how they prefer to pay.
Add the methods they already use: card tap, phone wallet, local QR payments.
Use a provider that works in your country, such as Stripe or Square where available.
Remove any step that is not needed, like retyping amounts or asking for paper details.
Watch the fees per method before you switch anything on.

sections.heading: Step 2: Look at split payments carefully
points: Check if your payment provider offers instalments or buy now pay later for your country.
Read who pays the fee, you or the customer, and what happens on refunds.
Check who carries the risk if the customer stops paying.
Only offer it on bigger items where it makes sense.
Be clear about the total price. Do not push anyone into debt.
This is education, not financial advice. Ask an accountant if unsure.

sections.heading: Step 3: Automate the sales log with Make.com
points: Trigger: a new successful payment from your provider (a Stripe module, or a webhook).
Action 1: add a row to Google Sheets with date, item, amount, fee and method.
Action 2: send a Slack or email message for orders above an amount you choose.
Action 3: a daily scenario that sums yesterday's sales and sends you one message.
Test with a small real payment first.
Watch for duplicate rows, refunds and failed payments. Add error handling so you get alerted.

sections.heading: Step 4: Run a two week test
points: Track checkout time, share of cash versus digital, and total fees.
Change one thing at a time so you know what worked.
Ask staff where customers get stuck.
Keep what saves time. Drop what only adds fees.

title: The Invoice Chaser Blueprint
summary: The three message templates, the timing, and the Make.com steps to send them automatically without chasing anyone who has already paid.

sections.heading: The 3-message sequence
points: Message 1, 1 day after the due date: the nudge. Friendly, short, assumes the invoice got buried.
Message 2, 7 days after: the specific ask. Request a payment date and invite any problem with the invoice.
Message 3, 14 days after: the firm close. State what you need, by when, and what happens next under your terms.
Change the tone at each step, not the facts. Same invoice number, amount and link every time.
Adjust the days to fit your payment terms. Treat 1, 7 and 14 as a starting point.

sections.heading: Message templates to copy
points: Message 1: Hi [Name], quick check on invoice [#] for [amount], due [date]. Here is the link in case it got buried: [link]. Shout if you need anything from me.
Message 2: Hi [Name], invoice [#] is now a week overdue. Can you confirm the payment date by [day]? If something looks wrong on the invoice, tell me and I will fix it today.
Message 3: Hi [Name], invoice [#] for [amount] is 14 days overdue. I need payment or a confirmed date by [day]. Call me if that is easier.
Add a consequence line to message 3 only if your contract supports it, for example pausing work on the project.
Keep every message under 60 words and include the link every time.

sections.heading: The Make.com build
points: Keep your invoices in one place, such as a Google Sheet with columns: client, email, invoice number, amount, due date, status, last message sent.
Trigger: a scheduled scenario that runs once a day, at a time that suits your clients.
Work out days overdue: today minus due date. Skip rows marked paid.
Add a Router with three routes and filters for 1, 7 and 14 days overdue. Each route sends its own template.
Send with the Gmail module, or your email tool, filling in name, invoice number, amount and link.
Write back to the sheet: which message was sent and when. This stops duplicates if the scenario runs twice.

sections.heading: Safety checks before it sends
points: Re-read the invoice status right before each send, not just at the start of the run. Someone may have paid in the meantime.
Add a pause column. Set it to yes for clients in a dispute or on a special arrangement, and filter those out.
Send message 3 to yourself first as a draft or approval email until you trust the setup.
Test with your own email address and fake invoices before pointing it at real clients.
Add an error notification so a failed run alerts you instead of failing quietly.

sections.heading: What to watch for
points: Wrong due dates in the sheet send the wrong message, so check the date format.
Late fees and interest rules vary by country and contract. Check yours before mentioning them.
Do not chase a client who has told you payment is on the way. Pause them manually.
Review the replies. The automation sends, but a person should answer.
This is education, not legal or financial advice.

title: The Approval Node Blueprint
summary: A two-scenario Make.com design for a money agent that drafts payments but cannot send them until a human approves. Includes the guardrails, the approval message and a test checklist.

sections.heading: The design in one picture
points: Scenario A (the drafter): trigger, agent, save draft, notify a human. It has no payment connection at all.
Scenario B (the payer): starts from a webhook, checks the draft, pays, logs. It is the only place payment credentials live.
The agent can be wrong, confused or tricked and still cannot pay, because it has nothing to pay with.
Keep the two scenarios separate. One scenario with an approval step in the middle is easier to bypass by mistake.

sections.heading: Build Scenario A: draft and ask
points: Trigger: whatever starts a payment in your business, such as an email with an invoice, a form, or a sheet row.
Add your AI module and ask for a fixed output: payee, amount, currency, reason, due date. Reject anything missing a field.
Add a Data store record with a unique ID, those fields, status = pending, and a created time.
Generate a random secret token and save it on the record. Do not use the record ID alone as the key.
Send the human a message by email or chat with the payee, amount, reason and two links: Approve and Reject.
Each link points to your Scenario B webhook with the record ID and the token.

sections.heading: Build Scenario B: approve, re-check, pay
points: Start with a custom webhook. Look up the record by ID.
Filter 1: status must still be pending. Filter 2: the token must match. Filter 3: the approval must not have expired.
Use a Router: Reject sets status = rejected and stops. Approve continues.
Re-check the amount and payee against the saved record, not against anything in the link.
Call your payment provider (an HTTP module or its Make app) using its test keys first.
Set status = paid, store the provider's reference, and notify the approver that it went through.

sections.heading: Guardrails that make it safe to sell
points: Hard cap per payment. Above it, require two different approvers.
Allowlist of known payees. A new payee always goes to manual review.
Expiry on approvals, such as 24 hours, so old links go dead.
Make the link open a confirm page first. Some email security tools open links automatically, which could approve by accident.
Log every proposal, decision, time and who approved. You want a trail if anyone asks.
Alert yourself when a scenario fails. A silent failure is worse than a loud one.

sections.heading: Test before real money
points: Run everything in your provider's test mode first.
Try to break it: click Approve twice, use an expired link, change the token, and send an amount over the cap.
Confirm that the second click does nothing and the others are blocked.
Start live with small amounts and a short allowlist, then widen it slowly.
This is education, not financial advice. Check your provider's terms and any rules that apply to your business.

title: The Fail-Closed Payout Blueprint
summary: A step-by-step pattern for letting an automation or AI agent trigger payouts in Make without handing it an open wallet. Based on the spend-cap and approval idea reported around Sunrate's Agentic Card. Education only, not financial advice.

sections.heading: 1. Write the rules before the scenario
points: List every payout type your business actually makes: supplier invoices, refunds, subscriptions, contractor fees.
For each, set a per-payment cap, a daily cap and a list of approved vendors. Use your own numbers.
Decide who approves what. One named person per band, plus a backup.
Store the rules in one place, like a Make Data store or a sheet, so you change limits without editing the scenario.
Keep a short 'never automate' list, such as new vendors or changed bank details.

sections.heading: 2. Build the gate in Make
points: Start every payout request with a webhook or a trigger that carries amount, vendor, currency and reason.
Look up the vendor and the caps from your rules store.
Add a Router with filters: auto-approve, needs human, blocked.
Make the last route a fallback that does nothing but log and alert. No match means no payout.
Check that missing or empty fields (amount blank, vendor not found) land in the blocked route, not the pay route.

sections.heading: 3. Add the human step
points: For mid-size amounts, send a Slack message or email with the amount, vendor, reason and two links: approve and reject.
Point each link at a second scenario's webhook so the decision comes back as data.
Set a timeout. No answer in your window means expired, not approved.
Make approvals single-use so a link cannot be clicked twice to pay twice.
Re-check the cap when the approval comes back, not only when the request went out.

sections.heading: 4. Make failure safe
points: Add error handlers on the payment module so a failure stops the run instead of retrying blindly.
Use an idempotency or reference key per request so a retry cannot pay the same invoice twice, if your payment provider supports it.
Alert a human on every blocked payout over a set amount.
Track the running daily total in your Data store and block when it hits the cap.
Enforce limits at the card or bank level too, so your workflow is not the only lock.

sections.heading: 5. Log it and test it
points: Log every request: time, amount, vendor, rule hit, approver, result.
Test with fake payouts first, or your provider's sandbox if it has one.
Try to break it: blank amount, huge amount, unknown vendor, duplicate request, expired approval.
Review the log weekly for the first month, then monthly.
Confirm what any real agent card or payment product actually enforces from its own documentation.

title: The KYC Doc-Triage Flow, Module by Module
summary: The full Make build for a document triage agent: what each module does, the flag rules to start with, how the human handoff works, and where it breaks. Education only, not compliance advice.

sections.heading: The flow, step by step
points: Trigger: Watch Files in a Folder (Google Drive or similar), or Watch Emails for attachments. One new file starts one run.
Log first: write a row (Airtable, Google Sheets or a Make data store) with file name, time received and a run ID before anything else happens.
Extract: send the file to an AI module and ask for fixed fields only: full name, date of birth, document number, address, expiry date. Ask for a confidence score per field.
Force structure: require JSON back. If the output is not valid JSON, send the file to the human route.
Look up the application: fetch the customer's submitted details from your CRM or sheet using the customer ID.
Compare, then Router: send the run down one of three paths: clean, flagged or error.

sections.heading: Flag rules to start with
points: Use plain filters for the judging. The AI extracts, the rules decide. Rules are easy to explain to an auditor, a model's mood is not.
Name: lowercase, strip accents and punctuation, then compare. Treat near matches (spelling variants) as flagged, not rejected.
Date of birth: must match exactly. Any difference is a flag.
Expiry date: earlier than today means flag. Also flag anything expiring very soon if your policy says so.
Proof of address: flag if the date is older than your policy allows (three months is a common starting point, use your own).
Confidence: any field below your threshold, or any missing field, is a flag. Start strict and loosen with data.

sections.heading: Route to a human
points: Clean path: add to a fast review queue. A person still signs off. Fast does not mean automatic.
Flagged path: post to Slack or Teams with the customer ID, the failed rules in plain words and a link to the file.
Make the decision a button or a form, not a chat reply. Approve, reject or request a new document.
Write the decision back to the log: who, when and why.
Error path: any module failure, bad JSON or unreadable scan goes to the human with the reason. Use Make's error handler so nothing disappears silently.
Never give the agent an approve action. It sorts and explains. People decide.

sections.heading: Where it breaks
points: Blurry or cropped scans: expect low confidence. That is the system working, so route it, don't retry forever.
Names: different spellings, order and transliteration cause most false flags. Review the first batch by hand and tune the name rule.
Customer data: before sending IDs to any AI provider, read its data terms and your own policy. Check how Make stores execution data in your scenario settings.
No log, no audit: if you can't show what was read and who decided, the build is not ready.
Test with fake or sample documents first. Get a compliance officer to review the rules before real customers touch it.

sections.heading: Why this one first
points: CIO Dive reported on 3 Nov that Accenture's research has 57% of banking executives expecting agents embedded in risk, compliance and audit within three years. It is a survey of expectations, not a guarantee.
Triage is reversible. A wrong flag costs a delay. A wrong payment costs money.
That makes it the easier thing for a bank to approve internally. This part is my opinion, not a forecast.
The same pattern (read, rule-check, route to a person, log) works for invoices, supplier onboarding and contract intake.

title: The Beach Day Blueprint: 3 Jobs Your Shop Can Do Alone
summary: Pick three repeat jobs, set up each one, and test it before you leave. Plain steps, no tech background needed.

sections.heading: Step 1: Find your three repeat jobs
points: Look back at last week's messages and tasks.
Write down anything you did three or more times.
Keep only the jobs where the answer is nearly the same every time.
Good picks: opening hours, prices, booking a time, sending an invoice.
Bad picks: refunds, complaints, custom quotes. Those stay with you.

sections.heading: Step 2: Job one, answer the same questions
points: Write your five most common questions and the best answer to each.
Keep every answer short and clear.
Save them as quick replies in WhatsApp Business or Instagram, if your account has that feature.
Set an away message for after hours that says when you will reply.
Add one line to each reply: 'For anything else, we will get back to you.'

sections.heading: Step 3: Job two and three, booking to invoice
points: Make a simple booking form (Google Forms or any form tool you already use).
In Make.com, start a new scenario. A scenario is a list of steps that run in order, like dominoes.
Step one is the trigger. It is the event that starts everything, such as 'new form answer'.
Add a step that puts the booking in your calendar.
Add a step that creates and sends the invoice from your invoicing tool.
Add a step that emails the customer a confirmation.

sections.heading: Step 4: Test it before you leave
points: Book a fake appointment with your own name and email.
Check that the calendar, invoice and email all show up correctly.
Turn on error alerts in Make.com so a broken step pings you.
Send anything unclear, such as odd questions or angry messages, to your own inbox.
Decide on one check-in time per day. Once is enough.
Do a short test run, such as a lunch break, before a whole day away.
